youtube_items.summary:
In Australia—and indeed other parts of the 
Western world—so-called ‘social cohesion’   is on a knife’s edge. You can feel 
a sense of unease gripping society. The ABC reported in August: “How extremism 
and foreign interference threaten Australian   social cohesion.” In September, The Age 
ran the headline: “Australia’s cohesion   is fraying. If we’re not careful, it may 
shatter.” While just this week, SBS noted:   “Royal Commission into the Bondi terror attack

youtube_items.title: [YT] Is inequality inevitable?
youtube_items.summary:
In South Africa, one of the most
unequal countries in the world, the richest one-tenth of 1%, owns 
almost 30% of all the country’s wealth, more than double what the bottom 90% owns. Income and wealth inequality are not new. In fact, economists and historians 
who’ve charted economic inequality throughout history haven’t found 
a single society without it. Which raises a bleak question: is inequality inevitable? One way to estimate inequality is 
with a number called the Gini index, which is calculated by comparing 
the income or wealth distribution of a perfectly equal society to the 
actual income or wealth distribution. The area of this shape multiplied
by 2 is the Gini index. A Gini of 1 indicates

analysis.problem: Social cohesion is under threat due to rising tensions and inequalities in various countries
analysis.root_cause: Underlying social and economic inequalities, exacerbated by factors like foreign interference and extremism
leverage_points: Government policies and initiatives to address social and economic disparities
International cooperation to mitigate the effects of foreign interference

proposed_actions.action: Implementing inclusive economic policies to reduce wealth gaps
proposed_actions.measurable_goal: 10% reduction in wealth inequality over the next 5 years

proposed_actions.action: Establishing community programs to promote social cohesion
proposed_actions.measurable_goal: 25% increase in community engagement and participation over the next 2 years

evidence: In Australia, social cohesion is on a knife’s edge due to rising extremism and foreign interference

analysis.generalization: This problem connects to the domains of human (social relations), civilization (economic inequality), and planet (resource distribution)
analysis.summary: Social cohesion is under threat due to rising tensions and inequalities, requiring government and international initiatives to address these issues. Implementing inclusive economic policies and community programs can help mitigate these effects.
